fieldsRead.text: Explore English language, literature and culture through language development, linguistics, British and other English-speaking literary traditions, and independent research. The English Language and Culture track is distinct from American Studies.

This UCR programme offers sustained literary interpretation, linguistic stylistics, creative expression, film and cultural history. These subjects respond to important parts of English Studies. Its language analysis and academic writing provide partial correspondences; it does not reproduce the dedicated English-proficiency, structural and historical linguistics curriculum or the full British literary-period sequence.

Both address linguistic description and analysis. UCR applies grammar, semantics, discourse and cognition to textual interpretation; this is a substantive part of introductory language analysis, not a complete general linguistics curriculum.

Both develop academic writing and presentation. UCR teaches scholarly-source evaluation, literature synthesis and research introductions alongside reflective and civic work; it does not reproduce English-specific proficiency assessment.

Both support research in literary studies. UCR applies critical perspectives in a textual research project; it does not cover the seminar’s full English-language-and-culture scope or replace the bachelor’s thesis.
Both study adaptation of literary texts across media. UCR concentrates on text-to-film analysis and adaptation theory; the selected external elective also includes stage adaptation.
First-year mentoring and the RADAr English diagnostic are required without EC. Attendance is compulsory for mentoring and first-year seminars; the first-year study-progress standard is 45 EC.
Both directly teach literary interpretation and critical reading; the UCR introduction covers more than English literature.
Both develop oral communication; UCR focuses on rhetorical argument rather than English-language proficiency.
The UCR course directly studies American popular-media narratives and social life, one important part of the British/American component; it does not supply British popular-culture coverage.

selectedDescriptionsRead.ACCPPDE101: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCLITR111: Introduction to Literary Studies introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation. Students examine what literature is, why it is read and studied, formal properties and the constructed character of texts. Fiction, poetry and drama are supplemented by contemporary nonfiction and basic film narration, developing critical terms, tools and techniques.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCCOMM111: The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSHIST111: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCLITR112: Provides a chronological overview of literature from the epic of Gilgamesh to post‑modernity. Reads literary and critical texts that explore human experience and teaches how to approach literature’s ambiguities and trace themes across ages.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCCOMM211: Style & Meaning studies stylistics: how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts and also in nonfiction. Students connect grammar, discourse and cognition with interpretation through frameworks for dialogue, narration, modality, deixis and text worlds. Analysis exercises lead to an original research-supported stylistic analysis.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSHIST112: Studies gender, storytelling and marginalised lives in the nineteenth- to twenty-first-century American context. Students examine slavery, community activism, representation and lived experience, using sources and projects that connect historical interpretation with contemporary questions.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCCOMM213: Develops persuasive speaking skills by applying rhetorical theory in the real world. Students work with local primary school children, building public-speaking skills and empowering them to find their voices.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCLITR211: World Myth & Literature compares mythic narratives across ancient and later traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes such as creation, power, gender, love and loyalty. Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic and African materials support literary analysis. A research paper, graphic explanation and creative retelling connect interpretation with narrative practice.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCMEDI111: Introduction to Film & Media examines how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, narrative and performance. Film history connects early cinema and major movements with feminist and postcolonial interpretation, alongside television, digital platforms and spectatorship. An analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory and scholarly research.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCMEDI112: Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSSOCI111: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCLITR212: Life & Travel Writing examines memoir, autobiography, diaries, personal essays, travel writing and digital self-presentation. Students explore memory, identity, autobiographical truth, ethics and cultural positioning through close reading and theory. A personal writing portfolio and an independent life-narrative project connect analysis with practice.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCMEDI211: From T.V. to TikTok examines American social history and everyday life from the mid-twentieth century through contemporary media. Television, film and digital forms connect storytelling and power with identity and imagined futures. Students compare dominant portrayals with Indigenous self-representation, investigate disability representation, and develop futures-oriented creative projects.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSHIST311: Native American Histories studies Indigenous social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, reciprocity and relational accountability guide collaboration with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders through arts-based work and a public-history project.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCMEDI312: Introduces documentary film from its early development to contemporary forms, analysing historical and social contexts, styles and genres, and ethical and aesthetic questions. Students analyse non-fiction representations and produce a short documentary item.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCLITR311: Film & Text studies relationships between literary and film narratives, adaptation and intertextuality. Students learn methods of film analysis and examine plot, character, setting, image, acting, music and sound, alongside the relationships among adaptors, critics and viewers.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCMEDI311: Media & Race investigates storytelling, power, privilege, resistance and systemic racism in American history from the late nineteenth century to the present. Film, photographs, music and other media connect past and present. Students produce research-based podcasts exploring how media sustains oppression and supports resistance.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSHIST211: History of Empires examines empires across global history and competing theories of empire. Students study expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. Historical cases, source analysis and an independent research essay connect theoretical interpretation with specific imperial experiences.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSSOCI214: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCLITR312: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.
selectedDescriptionsRead.MCCCOMM312: Creative Communication Laboratory combines close reading and creative workshops with poetry, rhythm, sound, voice and performance. Students develop traditional or hybrid creative projects grounded in scholarship and aesthetic traditions. Revision and reflection require them to explain their formal, conceptual and procedural choices.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSHIST312: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.
selectedDescriptionsRead.GOSPHIL311: Explores emotions from a philosophical perspective. Discusses nature and rationality of emotions, their role in ethics and art, and draws on historical and contemporary sources.
